newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania puts brave face on NATO rebuff by U.S.
newsitem.headline: Romania puts brave face on NATO rebuff by U.S.

text.p: Romania on Friday put a brave face on the U.S. decision that it be left out of the first wave of NATO's expansion, its finance minister saying the diplomatic setback would at least save money.

Opposition politicians were quick to blame the new centrist government for the failure of its high-profile campaign to win early admission to the alliance alongside Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic -- the countries favoured by Washington.
"It's a disappointment of course, but from my point of view, this means more money to allow us to cut taxes," Finance Minister Mircea Ciumara told reporters.
Romania's leaders have vowed to press on with their drive despite Washington's decision, which U.S. officials said was endorsed by President Bill Clinton and final.
Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea is due in Washington next week for a final push to win U.S. Senate backing and President Emil Constantinescu is to meet Kohl in Bonn on July 2.
"We've joined this race to win," Ciorbea told reporters after the U.S. announcement. "We're not going to give up now before Madrid."

Washington also left out the former Yugoslav republic of Slovenia, deemed another longshot prospect. Slovenian leaders have conceded that their chances of quick entry have now diminished but also vowed to maintain their campaign.

In France, an official source said French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl were considering an initiative to broaden the invitation to both states. Candidates are to be announced at next month's NATO summit in Madrid.
Former Romanian President Ion Iliescu, defeated in last November's election after seven years in power, said the government had instilled citizens with false hopes.

"The present leadership has made it seem as if failing to join in the first wave would spell catastrophe for Romania," said Iliescu, a former communist who now heads the opposition Party of Social Democracy.

While in office, Iliescu had also promoted quick entry to NATO but Western observers say the country's chances only became realistic after his defeat by Constantinescu and the adoption of serious reforms.

Hardline nationalists, now a small minority in the parliament, used the U.S. decision to blast the government over what they saw as concessions on longstanding border disputes in concluding treaties with neighbours Hungary and Ukraine.
"This was only to be expected. The West never really loved us," said Greater Romania Party leader Corneliu Vadim Tudor.
"Romania's leaders must have understood now that they should not put scissors to the country's map for the sake of joining a military alliance."

Romanian public opinion has always been heavily in favour of quick NATO membership but a survey published on Thursday showed Romanians were more concerned about their plunging living standards than joining the alliance.
A survey by independent pollsters IRSOP showed that 30 percent of those questioned saw no impact on Romania's future if the country failed to secure first-wave admission.

Sixty-two percent said their greatest fears were the effects of recent price increases imposed as part of the government's market reforms. Only nine percent said they feared most non-admission to NATO.
